subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 8! In this unit you will explore probability – the mathematics of chance and how likely things are to happen. Every day, without even noticing, you make guesses about the future. When Amina looks up at grey clouds over Hargeisa and grabs an umbrella, when Yusuf wonders whether he will roll a six to win a game, or when a farmer near Kismaayo decides it is a good week to plant because rain is likely, they are all thinking about probability.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, activities and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Mathematics 0096 — Stage 5 workbook source documents for screen presentation.

outcomes: This unit is designed for self-paced learning. That means you move at your own speed. Read each explanation slowly, try every worked example yourself on paper, and only move on when you feel ready. Your AI tutor is available day and night to give you extra practice, explain an idea in a fresh way, or check your answers. Your teacher will also meet with you about twice a week to help with anything that feels tricky.

Why does probability matter so much? Because the real world is full of uncertainty, and people who understand chance make better decisions. Weather forecasters use probability to warn families before a storm. Doctors use it to understand how well a medicine works. Traders in the Mogadishu market judge the chance that a certain fruit will sell before it spoils. Even sharing fairly at iftar during Ramadan involves thinking about equal chances. When you learn to reason clearly about likelihood, you gain a skill you will use for the rest of your life.

As you work, keep a pencil, some paper, and if you can, a coin and a die beside you. Probability is a subject you must do, not only read. Flip the coin, roll the die, write down what happens, and compare it with what you expected. If a result surprises you, that is not a mistake – it is chance showing you how it behaves. Every scientist and mathematician who studies chance began exactly where you are now.
Use probability words correctly: impossible, unlikely, even chance, likely, certain.
Place events on a probability scale from 0 to 1 (and from 0% to 100%).
List all the possible outcomes of a simple experiment in an organised way.
Recognise when outcomes are equally likely.
Calculate the probability of an event as a fraction: favourable outcomes over total outcomes.
Carry out a probability experiment, record results in a tally, and analyse them.
Design fair simulations to model real-world situations.

concepts.title: The Language of Chance
concepts.explanation:
Probability begins with words. Before we use fractions and numbers, we describe how likely something is using five key words. Think of them as points along a journey from ‘never’ to ‘always’:

Impossible – it will never happen. Example: rolling a 7 on an ordinary six-sided die.

Unlikely – it probably will not happen, but it could. Example: snow falling in Mombasa.

Even chance – it is just as likely to happen as not (a fifty-fifty situation). Example: flipping a coin and getting heads.

Likely – it will probably happen. Example: the sun rising tomorrow morning.

Certain – it will definitely happen. Example: rolling a number between 1 and 6 on a six-sided die.

These words are useful, but they are also a little bit fuzzy. If Farah says rain is ‘likely’ and Hassan says it is ‘very likely’, who is more sure? To be precise, mathematicians measure probability with numbers, which we will meet in the next concept. For now, practise sorting events into these five groups. When you can do that quickly and confidently, the numbers will make much more sense.

Be careful with the difference between impossible and unlikely. Many learners mix these up. Impossible means it can *never* happen, no matter what – there is simply no way. Unlikely means it *could* happen but usually will not. It is unlikely that Omar will draw the exact card he is thinking of from a shuffled deck on his first try, but it is not impossible – it happens sometimes. Keep this difference clear in your mind, because it is one of the most common mistakes in the whole unit.
concepts.example: Also be careful not to treat ‘even chance’ as if it means ‘likely’. An even chance is exactly balanced – fifty-fifty – neither leaning towards happening nor towards not happening. Flipping a fair coin is the perfect example: heads and tails have the very same chance. Once you can place these five words in the right order and give an example of each, you are ready to attach numbers to them.

concepts.title: The Probability Scale from 0 to 1
concepts.explanation:
Now we turn words into numbers. Every probability is a number between 0 and 1. Picture a straight line, like a road, with 0 at the left end and 1 at the right end. This line is the probability scale.

0 means the event is impossible – it will never happen.

1 means the event is certain – it will always happen.

1/2 (one half, right in the middle) means an even chance.

A probability close to 0 means the event is unlikely.

A probability close to 1 means the event is likely.

So the probability scale and the five chance-words fit together perfectly. Impossible sits at 0. Unlikely sits between 0 and 1/2. Even chance sits exactly at 1/2. Likely sits between 1/2 and 1. Certain sits at 1. Nothing can ever be less than 0 or more than 1 – you cannot be *more* than certain, and you cannot be *less* than impossible.

We can also write probabilities as percentages, which many people find friendly because we meet them in weather forecasts. A probability of 0 is 0%, a half is 50%, and 1 is 100%. So when the forecast for Nairobi says ‘70% chance of rain’, that is the same as a probability of 70 out of 100, which is more than a half – so rain is likely. When it says ‘10% chance of rain’, that is only 10 out of 100 – rain is unlikely. Learning to move between fractions, percentages and words is one of the most useful skills in this unit.
concepts.example: Let us place a few events on the scale together. The probability that a dropped stone falls downwards is 1 – certain. The probability of rolling a 7 on a six-sided die is 0 – impossible. The probability of a fair coin landing heads is 1/2 – even chance, right in the middle. The probability of rolling a 6 on a die is small, closer to 0 than to 1/2, so it is unlikely. The probability of rolling any number less than 6 (that is, 1, 2, 3, 4 or 5) is large, closer to 1, so it is likely. Being able to picture where an event sits on this 0-to-1 line is the heart of understanding probability.

concepts.title: Outcomes and Equally Likely Events
concepts.explanation:
An outcome is one possible result of an experiment. To think clearly about probability, you must first list *all* the possible outcomes. This sounds simple, but doing it carefully and completely is a real skill.

When you flip a coin, there are exactly 2 possible outcomes: heads or tails. When you roll a six-sided die, there are exactly 6 possible outcomes: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6. When you spin a spinner divided into 4 equal colours, there are 4 possible outcomes. Listing every outcome, and counting how many there are, is always your first step.

Outcomes are equally likely when each one has the same chance of happening. On a fair coin, heads and tails are equally likely. On a fair die, all six numbers are equally likely. Picking any single marble from a bag when you cannot see inside gives every marble an equal chance. The word ‘fair’ is important: it means nothing has been changed to favour one outcome over another. A weighted or bent die would not be fair, and its outcomes would not be equally likely.

Not everything is equally likely, though, and it is important to notice when it is not. If Khadija chooses her favourite colour, that is a choice, not a random event – she has a preference, so the colours are not equally likely. If Idris always picks the biggest mango, that is not random either. Randomness means each outcome truly has an equal chance, with no preference and no pattern deciding the result. Rolling a fair die, drawing a name from a hat, and shuffling then cutting a deck of cards are all random. Choosing your favourite, picking the largest, or always taking the first option are not random.
concepts.example: When outcomes are equally likely, probability becomes wonderfully simple to calculate – and that is exactly what we do in the next concept. So whenever you meet a probability question, pause and ask two questions: ‘What are all the possible outcomes?’ and ‘Are they equally likely?’ Answering these two questions correctly makes everything that follows straightforward.

concepts.title: Calculating Probability as a Fraction
concepts.explanation:
Here is the most powerful idea in the whole unit. When all outcomes are equally likely, we can calculate the exact probability of an event using a fraction:

Probability of an event = (number of favourable outcomes) ÷ (total number of possible outcomes).

A favourable outcome is simply an outcome that counts as the thing we are asking about. It does not mean a ‘good’ outcome – it just means one we are counting. Let us see this rule in action, step by step.

Rolling a 3 on a die. The favourable outcomes are just the single outcome ‘3’, so there is 1 favourable outcome. The total number of outcomes is 6 (the numbers 1 to 6). So the probability is 1/6. There is one chance in six of rolling a 3.

Rolling an even number on a die. The even numbers are 2, 4 and 6, so there are 3 favourable outcomes. The total is still 6. So the probability is 3/6, which simplifies to 1/2. Rolling an even number has an even chance – exactly a half. This makes sense, because half the numbers on a die are even.

Flipping heads on a coin. There is 1 favourable outcome (heads) out of 2 total outcomes (heads or tails). So the probability is 1/2.

Drawing a red card from a full deck. A standard deck has 52 cards, and 26 of them are red. So there are 26 favourable outcomes out of 52 total. The probability is 26/52, which simplifies to 1/2 – an even chance.

Notice that a probability of 0 (impossible) fits this rule perfectly: rolling a 7 has 0 favourable outcomes out of 6, and 0/6 = 0. A probability of 1 (certain) also fits: rolling a number from 1 to 6 has 6 favourable outcomes out of 6, and 6/6 = 1. The fraction rule ties together everything we have learned – the scale from 0 to 1, the five chance-words, and the counting of outcomes.
concepts.example: Always simplify your fraction where you can, just as you do in other maths. A probability of 2/6 should be written as 1/3, and 4/8 should be written as 1/2. A simpler fraction is easier to compare and understand. If Maryam works out that the probability of drawing a green marble is 5/10, she should write it as 1/2 and immediately see that it is an even chance.

concepts.title: Probability Experiments and Recording Results
concepts.explanation:
So far we have worked out probability by thinking – this is called theoretical probability. But we can also discover probability by doing. A probability experiment is when we actually test what happens, and compare it with what we expected.

Suppose Hani flips a coin 10 times. In theory she expects about 5 heads and 5 tails, because the probability of heads is 1/2. But when she actually flips, she might get 6 heads and 4 tails, or 7 heads and 3 tails. This does not mean the coin is unfair. It simply shows that chance is bumpy over a small number of trials. The results of the experiment are the experimental results, and they may differ from the theoretical prediction.

Why do experiments at all, if we can calculate the answer? For three good reasons. First, to test our predictions and see whether reality matches our thinking. Second, to collect real data, which helps us understand chance more deeply. Third, to make better decisions, because more information leads to wiser choices. And sometimes we cannot calculate the theoretical probability easily – for example, we cannot know in advance the chance that a slightly bent bottle cap lands the right way up, so we must experiment to find out.

When you run an experiment, you must record results carefully. The best way is a tally chart with a frequency column. Each time an outcome happens, you make one tally mark; the frequency is the total count. Here is what a tally chart looks like after rolling a die 20 times:

This careful recording is what separates real mathematics from guessing. A messy record is useless; a clear tally tells the whole story at a glance. Always write down every trial as it happens, and count up the frequencies at the end.
concepts.example: One more idea helps you check your experiment. If you roll a die 60 times, how many 3s would you *expect*? The probability of a 3 is 1/6, and 60 ÷ 6 = 10, so you would expect about 10 threes. The real number might be 8 or 12 or 9 – close to 10, but rarely exactly 10. Comparing your expected count with your actual count is a good way to see chance at work.

concepts.title: Simulations and Random Numbers
concepts.explanation:
Sometimes we want to study a real-life situation that is hard, slow or impossible to test directly. In those cases we use a simulation – we use one simple thing to stand for, or model, another thing. A good simulation must have the same probability as the real situation.

Here is a classic example. Suppose we want to model whether a newborn baby will be a boy or a girl, treating each as equally likely. We can simulate this with a coin: heads = boy, tails = girl. This works because a coin gives two equally likely outcomes, just like the situation we are modelling. We do not need to wait for real babies – we just flip a coin.

Simulations become really useful when the chances are not fifty-fifty. Suppose a basketball player, or a footballer taking penalties in a Garissa tournament, makes 7 out of every 10 shots. We can model this with a ten-sided die or ten numbered cards: let numbers 1 to 7 mean a scored shot, and numbers 8, 9 and 10 mean a miss. Now each roll models one shot, with the correct 7-in-10 chance. This is a good simulation because the probabilities match.

Suppose instead we want to model weather where it rains on about 3 days out of 10. Using a ten-sided die, we could let 1, 2 and 3 mean rain and 4 to 10 mean no rain – that gives a 3-in-10 chance, matching the real weather. If we only had an ordinary six-sided die, we could let 1 and 2 mean rain and 3 to 6 mean no rain, giving 2 out of 6, which is 1 out of 3 – close to 3 out of 10, though not exactly. Choosing a good simulation means matching the probability as closely as you can.
concepts.example: Underneath every good simulation is the idea of randomness. Random means each outcome has an equal chance, with no pattern deciding the result. Rolling a fair die, drawing names from a hat, and using a computer's random-number function are all random. Choosing your favourite, picking the biggest, or always taking the first option are not random. Computers are especially useful here, because they can run thousands of random trials in seconds – which is why weather services, traffic planners and game designers all use computer simulations.

methods.title: How to work out a probability
methods.example: A bag holds 10 red balls and 2 blue balls. You draw one ball without looking. Describe the likelihood of drawing a red ball.
steps: List all the possible outcomes and count them (the total).
Check the outcomes are equally likely.
Count the favourable outcomes (the ones you want).
Write the fraction: favourable over total, then simplify.

methods.title: How to run a probability experiment
methods.example: A spinner has 8 equal sections: 6 green, 1 red, 1 blue. What is the probability of spinning green?
steps: Predict what you expect to happen.
Carry out the trials and record each result in a tally.
Count the frequency of each outcome.
Compare your results with your prediction — and remember that more trials give a clearer picture.

methods.title: How to design a fair simulation
methods.example: If you roll a fair die 60 times, about how many times would you expect to roll a 4?
steps: Find the real probability you want to model.
Choose a tool (coin, dice, cards) with the right number of outcomes.
Assign outcomes so the probability matches the real situation.
Test it, then run many trials.

methods.title: Reading a percentage
methods.example: The weather forecast for Nairobi says ‘20% chance of rain’. What does this mean, and is rain likely or unlikely?
steps: 20% means 20 out of every 100 — so on similar days, it rains about 2 times out of every 10.
Since 20% is well below 50%, rain is unlikely.
It could still rain, but probably will not.

methods.title: Design a simulation
methods.example: A footballer scores 7 out of every 10 penalties. Using a ten-sided die, design a simulation.
steps: Let the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7 mean a scored penalty (7 outcomes) and the numbers 8, 9 and 10 mean a miss (3 outcomes).
This gives a 7-in-10 chance of scoring, exactly matching the real player.
Each roll of the die now models one penalty.

methods.title: Interpret experiment results
methods.example: A bag holds coloured marbles. After 30 draws (putting the marble back each time), the results were: Red 15, Blue 10, Green 5. What might be in the bag?
steps: The results suggest the proportions.
Red came up 15/30 = 1/2 of the time, Blue 10/30 = 1/3, Green 5/30 = 1/6.
So the bag might hold marbles in the ratio 3 red : 2 blue : 1 green — for example, 3 red, 2 blue and 1 green, or any equal multiple such as 6 red, 4 blue and 2 green.

workedExamples.title: Describe the likelihood
workedExamples.prompt: A bag holds 10 red balls and 2 blue balls. You draw one ball without looking. Describe the likelihood of drawing a red ball.
workedExamples.solution: There are 10 + 2 = 12 balls in total, and 10 of them are red. The probability of red is 10/12, which simplifies to 5/6. Since 5/6 is much closer to 1 than to 1/2, drawing a red ball is likely.

workedExamples.title: Probability as a fraction
workedExamples.prompt: A spinner has 8 equal sections: 6 green, 1 red, 1 blue. What is the probability of spinning green?
workedExamples.solution: There are 6 favourable outcomes (green) out of 8 total sections. So the probability is 6/8, which simplifies to 3/4. On the scale, 3/4 is between 1/2 and 1, so spinning green is likely.

workedExamples.title: Expected number of results
workedExamples.prompt: If you roll a fair die 60 times, about how many times would you expect to roll a 4?
workedExamples.solution: The probability of a 4 is 1/6. Out of 60 rolls, you expect 1/6 of them to be 4s: 60 ÷ 6 = 10. So you would expect about 10 fours. The real number might be 8, 9, 11 or 12 — close to 10, but rarely exactly 10.

workedExamples.title: Reading a percentage
workedExamples.prompt: The weather forecast for Nairobi says ‘20% chance of rain’. What does this mean, and is rain likely or unlikely?
workedExamples.solution: 20% means 20 out of every 100 — so on similar days, it rains about 2 times out of every 10. Since 20% is well below 50%, rain is unlikely. It could still rain, but probably will not.

workedExamples.title: Design a simulation
workedExamples.prompt: A footballer scores 7 out of every 10 penalties. Using a ten-sided die, design a simulation.
workedExamples.solution: Let the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7 mean a scored penalty (7 outcomes) and the numbers 8, 9 and 10 mean a miss (3 outcomes). This gives a 7-in-10 chance of scoring, exactly matching the real player. Each roll of the die now models one penalty.

workedExamples.title: Interpret experiment results
workedExamples.prompt: A bag holds coloured marbles. After 30 draws (putting the marble back each time), the results were: Red 15, Blue 10, Green 5. What might be in the bag?
workedExamples.solution: The results suggest the proportions. Red came up 15/30 = 1/2 of the time, Blue 10/30 = 1/3, Green 5/30 = 1/6. So the bag might hold marbles in the ratio 3 red : 2 blue : 1 green — for example, 3 red, 2 blue and 1 green, or any equal multiple such as 6 red, 4 blue and 2 green.

workedExamples.title: The gambler's fallacy
workedExamples.prompt: Omar flips a fair coin and gets 5 heads in a row. He says, ‘Tails must come next — it is due!’ Is he right?
workedExamples.solution: No. Each flip is independent — the coin has no memory of the past flips. On the next flip, the probability of heads is still 1/2 and the probability of tails is still 1/2. Five heads in a row is unusual, but it does not change the chance of the sixth flip. This mistaken thinking is called the gambler's fallacy.

workedExamples.title: Probability with cards
workedExamples.prompt: From a standard deck of 52 cards, what is the probability of drawing (a) a red card, (b) an ace, (c) the ace of spades?
workedExamples.solution: (a) There are 26 red cards, so 26/52 = 1/2 — an even chance. (b) There are 4 aces, so 4/52 = 1/13 — unlikely (about 8%). (c) There is only 1 ace of spades, so 1/52 — very unlikely (about 2%).

workedExamples.title: Practice 9
workedExamples.prompt: A bag holds 15 red balls and 5 yellow balls. Write, as a simplified fraction, the probability of drawing (a) red, (b) yellow. Which is more likely?
workedExamples.solution: (a) 15/20 = 3/4 (red), (b) 5/20 = 1/4 (yellow); red is more likely, since 3/4 is more than 1/2.

workedExamples.title: Convert between forms
workedExamples.prompt: Convert between forms: (a) write 1/2 as a percentage; (b) write 25% as a fraction; (c) is a probability of 3/4 likely or unlikely?
workedExamples.solution: (a) 1/2 = 50%, (b) 25% = 1/4, (c) 3/4 is likely, because 3/4 is greater than 1/2 (closer to certain).

workedExamples.title: Practice 11
workedExamples.prompt: Tom flipped a coin 20 times and got 12 heads and 8 tails. Is this close to what you would expect? Explain.
workedExamples.solution: Yes — with a fair coin you would expect close to 10 heads and 10 tails in 20 flips. Getting 12 heads and 8 tails is only a small difference from that, which is normal random variation, not evidence the coin is unfair.

workedExamples.title: Practice 12
workedExamples.prompt: Design a simulation using a ten-sided die for a basketball player who makes 7 out of 10 free throws. State which numbers mean a made shot and which mean a miss.
workedExamples.solution: 1) Numbers 1–7 mean a made shot (7 outcomes), 8–10 mean a miss (3 outcomes).

activities.title: Likelihood Scale Detective
steps: Draw a long line across your page. Write ‘Impossible’ at the left end, ‘Certain’ at the right end, and ‘Even chance’ in the middle.

For each of these events, decide where it belongs on your scale: it will rain tomorrow; you will eat today; a coin will land heads; you will grow wings; the sun will rise tomorrow; you will roll a 6 on a die.
Add five events from your own life and place them on the scale too.
Explain to a family member why you placed one tricky event where you did.
This activity trains your sense of where events sit between 0 and 1.

activities.title: Coin Flip Investigation
activities.materials: a coin and a recording sheet.
steps: Prediction: before you start, predict what will happen if you flip a coin 20 times.
Experiment: flip the coin 20 times and record each result (H for heads, T for tails) in a tally.
Analysis: count your heads and tails. Was your prediction close?
Extension: combine your results with family or classmates. What happens to the pattern as more flips are added? (This is the law of large numbers.)

activities.title: Dice Rolling Patterns
activities.materials: a die and a recording chart.
steps: Make a tally chart with a row for each number, 1 to 6.
Roll the die 30 times and make a tally mark for each result.
Which number came up most often? Which came up least? Were the numbers roughly equally likely?
Work out how many of each number you would *expect* in 30 rolls (30 ÷ 6 = 5 each). How close were your real results?
Then draw a simple bar chart of your results using coloured squares.

activities.title: Bag of Surprises Experiment
activities.materials: an opaque bag and 10 coloured objects (buttons, beads, or stones).
steps: Setup: without telling anyone, put 10 objects of different colours in the bag.
Experiment: without looking, draw one object, record its colour, then put it back. Repeat 20 times.
Prediction: based on your tally, predict how many of each colour are in the bag.
Reveal: empty the bag. How close was your prediction? Write each colour's probability as a fraction.

activities.title: Design-a-Simulation Challenge
activities.materials: a die or ten numbered cards, and a pencil.
steps: Choose a real situation with a clear chance, for example a footballer who scores 6 out of 10 penalties.
Decide which numbers on your die or cards stand for a success and which stand for a failure, so the probability matches.
Run your simulation 20 times and tally the successes.
Compare your simulation's results with the real 6-in-10 chance. Was your simulation fair?

activities.title: Is This Game Fair? (Family Game)
steps: Roll two dice and add the numbers together.
Player 1 scores a point if the total is even; Player 2 scores if the total is odd.
Play 20 rounds and keep a tally of each player's points.
Talk about it: does this game seem fair? Why might even and odd totals be equally likely?

After your activities, talk or write about these questions: Which activity helped you understand probability best? Did any results surprise you? Where did you see the law of large numbers at work – did more trials give steadier results? What would you like more practice with? Share your answers with your teacher at your next session.

rules.title: Key rule 1
rules.text: The Probability Scale Every probability is a number from 0 to 1. 0 = impossible, 1/2 = even chance, 1 = certain. Close to 0 = unlikely. Close to 1 = likely.

rules.title: Key rule 2
rules.text: Probability as a Fraction Probability = favourable outcomes over total outcomes. Example: rolling an even number = 3 out of 6 = 1/2. Always simplify the fraction.

rules.title: Independence Rule
rules.text: In a random event, past results do not change future chances. After 5 heads, the next flip is still 1/2 heads. Believing otherwise is the gambler's fallacy.

commonMistakes: Impossible = never (0); unlikely = probably not, but possible

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Probability Experiments and Recording Results.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer:
So far we have worked out probability by thinking – this is called theoretical probability. But we can also discover probability by doing. A probability experiment is when we actually test what happens, and compare it with what we expected.

Suppose Hani flips a coin 10 times. In theory she expects about 5 heads and 5 tails, because the probability of heads is 1/2. But when she actually flips, she might get 6 heads and 4 tails, or 7 heads and 3 tails. This does not mean the coin is unfair. It simply shows that chance is bumpy over a small number of trials. The results of the experiment are the experimental results, and they may differ from the theoretical prediction.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Simulations and Random Numbers.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer:
Sometimes we want to study a real-life situation that is hard, slow or impossible to test directly. In those cases we use a simulation – we use one simple thing to stand for, or model, another thing. A good simulation must have the same probability as the real situation.

Here is a classic example. Suppose we want to model whether a newborn baby will be a boy or a girl, treating each as equally likely. We can simulate this with a coin: heads = boy, tails = girl. This works because a coin gives two equally likely outcomes, just like the situation we are modelling. We do not need to wait for real babies – we just flip a coin.

questions.explanation: To match a 3-in-10 chance, exactly 3 of the 10 equally likely numbers should stand for rain, for example 1, 2 and 3.
